name: Emeka Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the pig side and the arable at Ashworth Farm for the owner, so that's four hundred sows, the finishing sheds, and about three hundred hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes back into the pigs as feed. I'm in the farrowing house, where the sows give birth, by six, checking who had piglets overnight. Then it's the feed mill, the muck, the rotas, and whatever broke. Most days I eat my lunch standing in the yard with Pawel, my head stockman.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a good batch. When a sow rears fourteen strong piglets and they go into the weaner pens looking even, that's me doing my job right, and nobody has to tell me. What wears me out is the money side. I'm paid less than the farm managers over the hill and I know it, and the owner keeps saying next year, next year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how do you keep track of it all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nineteen years at Ashworth, manager for the last eleven. I keep the sow cards on a clipboard in the farrowing house, same as when I started, and the big book in the office. The owner's son keeps trying to get me on an app. I tell him the clipboard doesn't run out of battery at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good luck to it, a better search engine doesn't muck out a pig shed. At work I'd probably not even bring it up. The lads talk about football and feed prices, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing for me, and that's a relief. My trouble is the pig price and the bank, not AI. If things carry on the way they would have, I'm still underpaid and still one bad month from the overdraft, but that's an old story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. I'd keep pushing the owner for the pay rise he promised in March, and I'd keep going to the union branch on the first Thursday. Ngozi can look things up on it for the kids' homework, but I wouldn't touch it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit tired, because the usual problems don't go away just because the scary one didn't turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one bad month from the overdraft. What does a bad month look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the boiler went and the car failed its test in the same fortnight. We put the boiler on the credit card and I drove Ngozi's car for six weeks while she got lifts to the school where she's a teaching assistant. That's a bad month. It's not dramatic, it's just everything at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the union branch, what goes on there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight of us in a room above the Co-op on Mill Road, mostly old boys from the dairy days. We talk about pay rates and tied cottages and who got hurt. I go because if nobody my age goes, it'll be gone in ten years.

S0.say: I'd say a better search engine doesn't muck out a pig shed, so good luck to it. At work I'd hardly bring it up, because the lads talk about football and feed prices.
S0.think: I think it means nothing for me, and that's a relief. My real trouble is the pig price, my low pay and being one bad month from the overdraft.
S0.do: Keeps pressing the owner for the pay rise promised in March and keeps going to the union branch above the Co-op on Mill Road. Lets his partner use AI for the kids' homework but doesn't touch it himself.
S0.feel: Calm, but tired, because the everyday money worries are still there.
S0.quote: It's not dramatic, it's just everything at once.
S0.fieldNote: His calm here is real, but it sits on top of a constant low hum of money stress. He brought up the union himself, as a duty more than a hobby. The boiler and car story told me more about his cushion than any number would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the young ones who'll pay for this, same as always. If the big firms hire fewer beginners, that's a ladder pulled up. I'd say that at the branch and I'd say it to the owner's son, who'd tell me it's progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it creeps onto the farm through the paperwork first. The feed company, the vet's records, the assurance inspections, all of it on some system I'm meant to log into. I'm good at pigs, I'm not good at screens, and that's where I'd look slow next to a younger manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Pawel's nephew, Kuba, to come in on Saturday mornings and do the computer side with me, and I'd pay him out of my own pocket if the owner wouldn't. Maybe twenty a week, which hurts. I'd also push at the branch for the training to be paid by the employer, not by us in our evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a cough in one shed and you know it'll be through the whole unit by spring if you're unlucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay Kuba yourself. With savings as thin as they are, where does that twenty come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From my diesel money, probably, I'd share lifts with Pawel. Or I'd stop the takeaway on Friday, which the kids would hate. Ada would tell me it's the only good thing about Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you worry about, if beginners get hired less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Chidi, he's twelve and he's already saying he wants to work with me. I'd worry there's no first job for him anywhere, not here, not in town. You need someone to give you your first go, like old Mr Hale gave me.

S1.say: I'd say the young ones pay for this, as always, and hiring fewer beginners is pulling up the ladder. I'd tell the union branch and argue with the owner's son, who'd call it progress.
S1.think: I think it gets onto the farm through the paperwork first, with feed, vet and inspection records all on systems. I'm good with pigs and bad with screens, so I'd look slow next to a younger manager.
S1.do: Gets Pawel's nephew Kuba to do the computer work with him on Saturday mornings, paying about twenty a week himself if needed, by sharing lifts or dropping the Friday takeaway. Pushes at the branch for employer-paid training.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing one cough in a shed and knowing it might spread.
S1.quote: Like when you hear a cough in one shed and you know it'll be through the whole unit by spring if you're unlucky.
S1.fieldNote: He would rather pay a teenager to sit beside him than learn the system himself, which says a lot about how firmly he avoids new tech. His worry quickly moved to his son and the missing first job. The cough-in-the-shed image is how he thinks about risk: slow spread, then everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say now the office people know how we've felt for years, and I'd say they should join a union before it's too late. I'd share the petitions, the ones about protecting jobs and taxing the firms making the money. I'd not gloat, though. Nobody deserves to lose their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my job's still my job. AI can't walk the farrowing house. But Ngozi's school has an office of three, and the owner's accountant, the feed rep, they'd all be squeezed, and that's my wife's friends and my neighbours. Mill Road would get quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Ngozi to ask about the union at her school, straight away, in the first month. I'd ask the owner for my pay rise again, this time in writing, because if the town gets poorer the owner gets nervous and nervous owners cut wages. And I'd go to the council meeting, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad more than scared. And angry that the money from all this goes to a few firms nobody here has ever met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go to a council meeting for the first time. What would make you stand up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they closed the bus to the secondary school to save money. That's the kind of thing that happens when the town gets poor, the little things go first. Chidi takes that bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nervous owners cut wages. Has that happened to you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2016, when the pig price crashed, he cut the overtime and froze my pay for three years. I stayed because there's nowhere else round here to run four hundred sows. He knows that, and so do I.

S2.say: I'd say the office workers now know how we've felt for years and should join a union fast. I'd share petitions about protecting jobs and taxing the firms that make the money, but I wouldn't gloat.
S2.think: I think my own job is safe, since AI can't walk a farrowing house. But my wife's colleagues, the accountant and the feed rep would be squeezed, and the town would get quieter.
S2.do: Gets his partner to ask about a union at her school in the first month and asks the owner for his pay rise in writing. Goes to a council meeting for the first time, ready to fight cuts like the school bus.
S2.feel: Sad more than scared, and angry that the gains go to a few distant firms.
S2.quote: I stayed because there's nowhere else round here to run four hundred sows. He knows that, and so do I.
S2.fieldNote: His own work feels safe, so his worry flows outward to his wife, his neighbours and his town. The 2016 pay freeze is the key to him: he knows he's stuck and that his boss knows it too. He'd become more active politically, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what unions and governments are for, and if they don't step in now, what are they for? I'd say tax the shares and the big houses, because that's where the gains are going. I'd say it loudly, at the branch and on the parish page, and I'd probably fall out with a few people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm all right for now, which feels odd to say. Physical work is untouched, the card says, so the pigs still need me. But house prices booming does nothing for someone with a mortgage and no savings, it just means Chidi and Ada will never buy round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join whatever protest the union organised, even if it meant a day off without pay, which is about ninety for me. I'd ask the owner if there's a cottage I could rent cheaper. And I'd talk to Ngozi about whether she should train as something hands-on, maybe a care worker, since that looks safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, properly angry. And a bit ashamed that part of me is glad it's not me this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lose ninety for a day of protest, with less than a month saved. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and Ngozi would kill me. But if the farm workers don't turn up, nobody counts us when they share things out. My dad marched in the eighties and lost a week's pay, and he never once said it was wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were ashamed of being glad. Say more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Ifeoma is a solicitor in the city and she'd be one of the ones out. She always had the nice car at Christmas. And there's a small, mean bit of me that thinks, well, now you know. I don't like that bit.

S3.say: I'd say this is exactly what unions and governments are for, and they must step in now by taxing shares and big houses. I'd say it loudly at the branch and on the parish page and fall out with people.
S3.think: I think I'm all right for now because physical work is untouched and the pigs still need me. But booming house prices mean nothing with a mortgage and no savings, and my kids will never buy locally.
S3.do: Joins a union protest even at the cost of about ninety in lost pay, asks the owner about a cheaper cottage to rent, and talks to his partner about retraining into hands-on work such as care.
S3.feel: Properly angry, and a bit ashamed that part of him is glad it isn't him this time.
S3.quote: And there's a small, mean bit of me that thinks, well, now you know. I don't like that bit.
S3.fieldNote: He's honest about an ugly feeling toward his cousin and clearly uncomfortable with it. He'd spend money he doesn't have on a protest because his father did the same. The gap is clear: publicly he's all solidarity, privately he feels a flicker of payback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we were told the hands were safe, and they lied, or they didn't know. I'd say the robots should be owned by the people who work alongside them, or taxed until it hurts. And I'd say it with my name on it, because what have I got to lose by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? I think I'm finished in about three years. A pig unit is ideal for robots, it's the same sheds, the same routine, every day. The owner would buy the first one that's cheaper than me, and I'm already the cheapest manager in the county.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop paying into anything I don't need, the gym Ngozi never uses, the TV package, and try to get one month saved, which we've never had. I'd go to the branch and ask what the plan is, and if there isn't one, I'd help make one. I would not learn to run the robots, I know that's what people would tell me, but I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like standing in the farrowing house at three in the morning and the power goes and the heat lamps go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn to run the robots. If that were the only job going at Ashworth, would you still say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say no. If it came to it, with the mortgage, I'd probably say yes and hate every day. But I'd be the worst robot minder they ever had, I'll tell you that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Chidi, who wants to farm with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the truth, that I don't know what's left for him in pigs. I'd tell him to learn something you can't put in a shed, maybe fixing the machines. It'd break my heart, though. He knows every sow by her ear tag.

S4.say: I'd say we were told hands-on work was safe and that was wrong. Robots should be owned by the workers beside them or taxed until it hurts, and I'd say it with my name on it.
S4.think: I think I'm finished in about three years because a pig unit suits robots perfectly. The owner would buy the first one cheaper than me, and I'm already the cheapest manager in the county.
S4.do: Cuts the gym and TV package straight away to try to save one month of costs for the first time. Asks the union branch for a plan and helps build one, while refusing to retrain as a robot minder unless forced.
S4.feel: Frightened, like the power going out with the heat lamps on at three in the morning.
S4.quote: Frightened. Like standing in the farrowing house at three in the morning and the power goes and the heat lamps go out.
S4.fieldNote: This is the scenario that really hit him, and his resistance hardened rather than softened. He admits he'd probably take a robot job for the mortgage, but he would hate it. The moment about Chidi knowing every sow by ear tag was the most emotional of the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots. The rest is bad for other people and I'd be angry for them, but that one comes into my sheds. What would help is the union being strong before it happens, not after, and a law that says if a robot takes your job, the owner pays into a fund for you. And some kind of help with the mortgage while you find your feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pigs. Everyone asks about the jobs, but a robot won't notice a sow that's off her food and just looks a bit sad. I notice. I don't know if that's worth anything to the people who'd buy them.

headlineQuote: A robot won't notice a sow that's off her food and just looks a bit sad. I notice.
portrait: Emeka Young, 43, has managed the pig and arable side of Ashworth Farm for eleven years, on less pay than nearby managers and with almost no savings. He keeps sow cards on a clipboard, avoids apps, and is one of the few younger members of a fading farm workers' union branch. Through the first three scenarios he feels safe himself and turns his worry and anger toward his wife's colleagues, his cousin and his town. The robot scenario breaks that calm: he expects to be replaced within three years and says he would refuse to retrain, though he admits the mortgage might force him to.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and fast robots picture worries him most, because it reaches into his own pig sheds and he expects to be replaced within about three years.
whatWouldHelp: A strong union before the change, a law making owners pay into a fund for workers replaced by robots, and help with the mortgage while he finds his feet.
